newsitem.title: USA: U.S. NOAA researcher-"el Nino" strengthened in May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. NOAA researcher-"el Nino" strengthened in May.

text.p: Warm ocean temperatures off the western coast of South America have triggered an "El Nino" weather pattern that could have a significant impact on crop production around the world, a U.S. official said Tuesday.

"We do have an El Nino in progress," Vern Kousky, a research meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's climate prediction center, told Reuters. "It strengthened further in May. Water temperatures are quite warm out there."

An el Nino can have a profound effect on global weather patterns for as long as 18 months, depending on how rapidly ocean temperatures return to normal. The last major el Nino was in late 1991 through mid-1992 and a less severe one occured in 1994-95.

This latest one is already leading to dryer than normal conditions in Indonesia and other parts of Southeast Asia. This summer's rainfall in India should also be "less than average" because of a weaker than normal monsoon, Kousky said.

The weather pattern could also lead to "wetter than normal" conditions in parts of the U.S. Midwest this summer, Kousky said. But "it's very hard to get a clear signal" for U.S. summer weather patterns from an el Nino, he said.

However, the el Nino could lead to warmer-than-normal and possibly dryer-than-normal conditions in the upper Midwest and Northern Great Plains next winter, Kousky said. That could hurt this fall's U.S. winter wheat crop, he said.
The el Nino could also reduce fishing catches off the west coast of South America as those fish move to cooler waters and reduce the salmon run off the Western U.S., he said.
